--- title: "Model Validation" subtitle: "Lecture 12" author: "Vivek Srikrishnan" course: "BEE 4750" institution: "Cornell University" date: "October 07, 2026" format: revealjs: slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all center-title-slide: true width: 1280 height: 720 transition: none toc: true toc-depth: 1 toc-title: "Overview" history: false link-external-newwindow: true theme: ../sass/slides.scss template-partials: - title-slide.html menu: numbers: true html-math-method: mathjax include-in-header: mathjax-config.html date-format: long email-obfuscation: javascript chalkboard: theme: whiteboard buttons: true controls: true engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11.5"] execute: freeze: auto daemon: 600 --- # Review of Last Class ## The Grid Is a Choice We Make The plume equation gives a concentration at **every** point. A grid is how we look at it, and looking is not free: Finer grids mean more resolution (and more accurate assessments) but take more computation and memory. ## The Peak Is Sensitive To A Number Of Factors The ground-level peak is downwind from the stack because the plume has to spread down to the ground first. A taller stack lowers the peak and pushes it further out: the same emissions, spread over more distance. Three stacks that each comply with a regulation can jointly violate, and the combined maximum sits where **no single plume** peaks. ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # When Should We Trust A Model? ## A Model Gave You a Number A model will always give you a number. It is a machine that takes inputs and produces outputs. Someone asks: **why should I believe this?** ## Sources of Model Error ::: {.incremental} 1. **Numerical**: the equations are right, the grid or step size is too coarse. *You control it: a trade-off with computation.* 2. **Parametric**: the structure is right, the parameter values are wrong. *Treated by calibration, which has standard traps.* 3. **Structural**: the model is the wrong model for this system. *Not always obvious, nor always fixable.* ::: No amount of refinement fixes the last two. # Model Calibration: Fitting to Data ## Calibrating the DO Model $k_a$, $k_c$, and $k_n$ are not constants of nature. They depend on the river: its turbulence, its temperature, what is actually in the waste. They are also influenced by the other factors we do not include in the model: the other oxygen sinks, the other oxygen sources, and the other processes that affect them. In practice you do not rely on lab measurements, you **measure dissolved oxygen in the field and fit the rates to it**. ## The Data We Would Actually Have ::: {#cell-fig-calibration-data .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Seeded so the lecture reports the same numbers every time it renders. Random.seed!(3) observation_step = 8 # one observation every 2 km on a 0.25 km grid truth = simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, true_params) observation_index = 1:observation_step:length(truth) observation_distance = [(i - 1) * Δx for i in observation_index] observations = truth[observation_index] + rand(Normal(0, 0.2), length(observation_index)) p_data = scatter(observation_distance, observations, color=cb_vermillion, markersize=7, xlabel="Distance downstream [km]", ylabel="DO [mg/L]", label="measurements", legend=:bottomright) plot!(p_data, 0:Δx:river_length, truth, color=:black, linewidth=4, label="model that generated them") plot!(p_data, size=(1100, 430), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm) ``` ::: {#fig-calibration-data .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Twenty-one dissolved oxygen measurements, every 2 km, against the model that generated them. ::: ::: ## Scoring Rules ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} rmse(simulated, observed) = sqrt(mean((simulated .- observed).^2)) function do_rmse(ka, kc, kn) candidate = (; ka, kc, kn, B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0, Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U) simulated = simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, candidate) return rmse(simulated[observation_index], observations) end ``` ::: A **scoring rule** scores how closely the model matches the measurements. A common (and typically good!) choice: ::: {.small-math} $$\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y^\text{sim}_i - y^\text{obs}_i\right)^2}$$ ::: Lower is better; zero is **impossible in real life**. The true rates score 0\.18; a naive start, all rates 0.5, scores 1\.02. ## Optimizing RMSE ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="false" code-line-numbers="|1-3|5-7"} lower_bounds = [0.05, 0.05, 0.05] upper_bounds = [2.0, 2.0, 2.0] initial_guess = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] calibration = Optim.optimize(v -> do_rmse(v[1], v[2], v[3]), lower_bounds, upper_bounds, initial_guess) fitted = Optim.minimizer(calibration) @show fitted; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fitted = [0.6106236141326572, 0.34699675218765863, 0.3469967525444313] ``` ::: ::: ## The Calibrated Fit ::: {#cell-fig-calibrated-fit .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} fitted_params = (; ka=fitted[1], kc=fitted[2], kn=fitted[3], B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0, Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U) p_fit = scatter(observation_distance, observations, color=cb_vermillion, markersize=7, xlabel="Distance downstream [km]", ylabel="DO [mg/L]", label="measurements", legend=:bottomright) plot!(p_fit, 0:Δx:river_length, truth, color=:black, linewidth=4, label="true model") plot!(p_fit, 0:Δx:river_length, simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, fitted_params), color=cb_blue, linewidth=3, linestyle=:dash, label="calibrated model") plot!(p_fit, size=(1100, 430), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=8mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm) ``` ::: {#fig-calibrated-fit .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` The calibrated model against the measurements. It passes through the data at least as well as the truth does. ::: ::: ## We Recovered the Wrong Rates | | True | Calibrated | |:--|--:|--:| | $k_a$ reaeration | $0.60$ | 0\.61 | | $k_c$ CBOD decay | $0.40$ | 0\.35 | | $k_n$ NBOD decay | $0.25$ | 0\.35 | | RMSE (mg/L) | 0\.18 | 0\.16 | ::: {.fragment .fade-in} The decay rates came back **identical**, and the truth fits *worse* than the calibration. Three free parameters chasing 21 noisy points will essentially never recover the truth. ::: ## Why Are CBOD and NBOD Non-Unique? ::: {#cell-fig-rmse-valley .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} cbod_rates = 0.10:0.01:0.80 nbod_rates = 0.05:0.01:0.60 error_surface = [do_rmse(0.6, kc, kn) for kn in nbod_rates, kc in cbod_rates] p_valley = contourf(cbod_rates, nbod_rates, error_surface, color=:viridis, linewidth=0, xlabel="CBOD decay rate [1/d]", ylabel="NBOD rate [1/d]") scatter!(p_valley, [0.4], [0.25], color=:white, markersize=11, markershape=:star5, label="truth", legend=:topright) scatter!(p_valley, [fitted[2]], [fitted[3]], color=cb_vermillion, markersize=9, label="calibrated") plot!(p_valley, size=(1050, 300), left_margin=12mm, right_margin=10mm, bottom_margin=12mm, top_margin=5mm) ``` ::: {#fig-rmse-valley .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` RMSE in mg/L over the two decay rates, with reaeration held at its true value. The minimum is a trough, not a point. ::: ::: The data see only the **sum** of two decays: faster CBOD with slower NBOD gives nearly the same sag. ## How Does Noise Influence the Fit? ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Score a candidate against any set of measurements, not just the ones above. function rmse_against(ka, kc, kn, measured) candidate = (; ka, kc, kn, B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0, Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U) simulated = simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, candidate) return rmse(simulated[observation_index], measured) end # Nothing about the river changes across these refits. The only difference is # which measurements we happened to take. n_refits = 8 refit_ka = zeros(n_refits) refit_kc = zeros(n_refits) refit_kn = zeros(n_refits) for seed in 1:n_refits Random.seed!(seed) draw = truth[observation_index] + rand(Normal(0, 0.2), length(observation_index)) result = Optim.optimize(v -> rmse_against(v[1], v[2], v[3], draw), lower_bounds, upper_bounds, initial_guess) best = Optim.minimizer(result) refit_ka[seed] = best[1] refit_kc[seed] = best[2] refit_kn[seed] = best[3] end ``` ::: | Rate | True | Lowest | Highest | Spread | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:| | $k_a$ reaeration | $0.60$ | 0\.58 | 0\.61 | 0\.03 | | $k_c$ CBOD decay | $0.40$ | 0\.32 | 0\.45 | 0\.13 | | $k_n$ NBOD decay | $0.25$ | 0\.2 | 0\.35 | 0\.15 | ::: {.fragment .fade-in} **Non-identifiability**: the data constrain a *combination* of the rates, not each rate on its own. ::: # Positive and Negative Controls ## We Just Ran a Positive Control Data from **known** parameters: a test with a known right answer, run on the procedure rather than on the system. ::: {.incremental} - The procedure fits the data. It does **not** recover the parameters. - The failure is not a bug. It is a property of this model and this data. - We only know that because we knew the answer in advance. **Real data is always messier**. ::: ## Negative Control: Fitting Pure Noise ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Same procedure, but the "measurements" are noise about a flat line --- # there is no sag here for any parameter set to explain. Random.seed!(11) flat_observations = fill(mean(observations), length(observation_index)) + rand(Normal(0, 0.2), length(observation_index)) function noise_rmse(ka, kc, kn) candidate = (; ka, kc, kn, B0=true_params.B0, N0=true_params.N0, Cs=true_params.Cs, U=true_params.U) rmse(simulate_do(C0, river_length, Δx, candidate)[observation_index], flat_observations) end noise_fit = Optim.minimizer(Optim.optimize(v -> noise_rmse(v[1], v[2], v[3]), lower_bounds, upper_bounds, initial_guess)) @show round.(noise_fit; digits=2); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` round.(noise_fit; digits = 2) = [0.41, 0.1, 0.19] ``` ::: ::: A **negative control** feeds the procedure something with no signal in it. If a calibration reports confident parameters when handed noise, its confident parameters mean nothing. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} An optimiser always returns its argument minimum. **Getting an answer is not evidence that there was one.** ::: # Validation: Trusting A Model ## Calibration Is Not Validation Following @Oreskes1994-br: - **Calibration**: choosing parameters so simulations match observations. - **Validation**: establishing that the model is a legitimate basis for the claim you want to make. ## Two Kinds of Evidence ::: {.incremental} - **Empirical validity**: does it predict data it has never seen? Hold observations back; do not fit them. - **Face validity**: do the included processes make sense? the parameterizations? ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} These can fail independently. A model can predict well for the wrong reasons, or be mechanistically partially right but fail to predict. ::: ## A Plume With a Missing Sink The engineer's Gaussian plume has no sinks: everything emitted stays in the air. Real SO$_2$ is removed in transit: **oxidation** to sulfate (about 2% per hour) and **deposition** to dew-wet ground (fast under a shallow night-time plume). Together, about 52% per hour of travel. ::: {.notes} The model is the right kind of model, a Gaussian plume on a stable night, but it leaves out a process: nothing removes SO2 between the stack and the receptor. In reality SO2 is oxidised to sulfate, slowly, at a few percent per hour, and it deposits onto the ground. Deposition is the bigger sink here: a deposition velocity of about a centimetre per second into a plume only about fifty metres deep removes it quickly. Deposition at night can be lower when plants close their stomata, and higher onto dew-wet surfaces, so treat the exact rate as an assumption for the example. The point is that this is a structural error: no value of the model's parameters adds a sink. ::: ## Can We Calibrate Our Way Out? ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function wind_rmse(wind_speed) trial = (; plume_params..., wind=wind_speed) modelled = [ground_concentration(monitor_downwind[i], monitor_crosswind[i], class_F, trial) for i in 1:n_monitors] return rmse(modelled, monitor_observed) end wind_fit = Optim.optimize(v -> wind_rmse(first(v)), [0.3], Float64[20], [2.5]) fitted_wind = first(Optim.minimizer(wind_fit)) ``` ::: Wind speed is uncertain, and the whole field scales as $1/u$: the obvious knob. Calibrated wind: 3\.2 m/s. RMSE falls from 287 to 115 µg/m³ (38% to 15% of the mean observation). ::: {.fragment .fade-in} A good fit. But the anemometer read **2.5 m/s**. ::: ## Monitors We Did Not Fit | Monitor | Observed (µg/m³) | Calibrated model (µg/m³) | Error | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | 8 km | 531 | 663 | +25% | | 10 km | 270 | 537 | +99% | The inflated wind dilutes the whole plume by one constant factor; the sinks remove more SO$_2$ the further it travels. The calibration matched the monitors it saw by getting the wind wrong. ## So What Would Have Caught It? Calibration made the fit good and left the model wrong. ::: {.incremental} - **Face check**: the calibrated wind contradicts the anemometer. And are all the SO$_2$ sinks in the model? - **Empirical check**: test the calibrated model on data it was not fitted to, and plot its residuals rather than trusting one number. ::: # Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule ## Key Takeaways ::: {.incremental} - **A model that fits better can be more wrong.** Calibration minimises a metric, not error in the parameters. - **Nonuniqueness is normal.** Compensating processes mean data often constrain a *combination* of parameters. - **A good fit is not validation.** Check calibrated parameters against what you know, and test on data you did not fit. - **Controls test the procedure**, not the system: positive asks whether it can recover a known answer, negative asks whether it invents one. - **Empirical and face validity fail independently.** ::: ## The Whole Arc, Once More ::: {.incremental} - Forward Euler: error $O(\Delta t)$ --- halve the step, halve the error. - Monte Carlo: error $O(n^{-1/2})$ --- quadruple the samples, halve the error. - A grid on a closed form: the samples are exact; the error is in what you ask of them. - **Calibration: the error does not shrink with effort at all.** More optimisation makes the fit better and the parameters no more true. ::: ## Next Classes **Monday**: Fall Break --- no class. **Wednesday, Oct 14**: Decision models and linear programming. The second half of the course moves from *describing* systems to *prescribing* what to do about them. ## Assessments **HW5**: assigned today, due Thursday Oct 15. Gaussian plumes and model validation. **Quiz 3**: Wednesday Oct 21. # Appendix ## Why Compensating Processes Make a Valley Both oxygen sinks decay exponentially in distance: $$k_c B_0 e^{-k_c x/U} + k_n N_0 e^{-k_n x/U}$$ Over the stretch where measurements exist, raising $k_c$ and lowering $k_n$ leaves this sum nearly unchanged. The data constrain the sum; they do not separate the terms. Reaeration is different in kind --- it pulls toward $C_s$ rather than away --- so $k_a$ stays identifiable. ## The Lake, Revisited Homework 3 asked what happens when a manager uses a one-stock lake model that ignores sediment recycling entirely. That is structural error, met before we had a name for it: the fitted model is internally consistent and still sets an unsafe loading. ## References
